doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Pomona College audition and bringing Bobby Bradford in
summary: Woodshedding flute with James Newton for the audition, then petitioning to replace the Dixie-style stage band director with Bobby Bradford.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah. Okay. Well let’s talk about your progression as a musician a little bit. You had mentioned that to get into college you had to do some woodshedding with something that—

James Newton. I had to do some woodshedding with James Newton to really get my flute chops together. Because I had a flute, I played it “Memphis Underground” or something, real light kind of flute stuff. Well I mean not light but, yeah light.
Well you didn’t have to have the greatest tone and all that.

Yeah. I was no good on the flute. And I played piccolo in the marching band. I was no good. The tenor was my M.O. So anyway I had to work on a — anyway I knew all my scales and all that kind of stuff, but they just didn’t sound the same on flute you know? So James, when I went down to Pomona to the black pre-freshman program, I got with James and I said, “Look, this is what I have to do for this audition.” So we went through it, and okay, we’ll work on a few things. We’ll work on this Debussy thing and then we’ll work on this Fauré. And it worked out really well. And I passed. And I was so happy. And so as soon as I got into Pomona, the first thing I did was I got the big band director fired somehow. Well the guy, we had a little money that they had saved up from the year before, and the guy decided that they wanted to invest it in some armbands for the big band. And some of those hats, the little straw hats.
It’s not that long ago, you know, this is ’73 you know. But I was like, I said to the cats.
Oh I’m sorry to interrupt you.

Yeah, they’re like garters. So they wanted to go on this Dixie thing. And I was like oh man, I was the only guy that — well I was the only black guy that was in the stage band. So I said well look, I went to the director, Mr. Russell, to the head of the music department. I said you know this is not really jazz what this guy’s trying to do. And I

don’t even know this guy, but I think that we need a real jazz guy if we’re going to have a jazz stage band. So I suggested that he maybe should interview Bobby Bradford and John Carter. But John Carter was already teaching and so was Bobby, he was teaching at Pasadena CC and at another college. And John Carter was teaching at another college in Carver. So Bobby came in. He did an interview, and you know Bobby Bradford is great. He’s a great educator. So Bobby got the gig. He just retired last year. And it got to be well known that people would come from other schools to be in that stage band after Bobby had really got the program on the road. So I was always happy that I was responsible for making the petition to get the other guy fired, to get Bobby in place, so that we could actually have jazz at Pomona College. And now they’re proud of it. They’re proud of the fact that they had jazz. That was the beginning of jazz at Pomona College.
I see. Otherwise they were doing the Dixieland routine.
We were going to die in there man. You know now, kids aren’t going to go for that. Kids, they would never do that now, kids.
